name: Hoodingmaxxing

card.summary: A set of eye-area tricks, from cold exposure to eyebrow-raising to eyelid surgery, aimed at giving the upper eyelid a hooded, deeper-set look.
card.note: Methods range from DIY cold exposure, which has not been studied for this purpose, to surgery and fillers done by clinicians.

quick.overview:
Hoodingmaxxing is the community term for increasing or showing upper-eyelid hooding, where a fold of skin or fat sits over the lid crease. Some forum members consider a hooded, deeper-set eye area attractive and want more of it, especially if they have prominent or exposed eyes.

The most discussed method is applying ice or cold water to the eye area so that it looks puffier for a while. Other methods include raising the eyebrows to let fat slide onto the lid, eyelid fillers, and surgery. Posters report temporary changes; no published study has tested ice for this purpose.
quick.how: People describe holding ice cubes or cold water against the eye area for a few minutes a day and checking the effect in photos. Others use a facial expression (brows raised, eyes looking up) to let tissue settle over the lid. Fillers and surgery are done by clinicians and are described mainly as things people wish were available.
quick.risks: Cold applied to skin can cause redness or irritation, and prolonged ice contact can injure skin. Eyelid fillers and surgery carry the usual medical risks and are performed by specialists; some oculoplastic surgeons are described by forum members as reluctant to treat the upper lid with filler.

lead: Hoodingmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for deliberately increasing or exposing upper eyelid hooding, in which a fold of skin or fat overhangs the lid crease. Practitioners usually seek a deeper-set, more shaded look to the eyes, often when their own upper eyelids look flat or the eyes look exposed [1][3].

The best-known technique is "ice hooding". One looksmax.org guide proposes that cold exposure around the eyes stimulates fat storage in the region, and compares it with ice baths and cold therapy advocated by figures such as Wim Hof and Jack Kruse [1]. Another poster describes placing ice cubes on the eye area for two to five minutes daily for a few weeks and reports a temporary "pump" with more lid cover [3].

A later thread in the same community suggests a simpler method: raising the eyebrows and looking up so fat slides onto the lid, which the poster says can last for hours, and treats ice methods as a fallback [2]. Replies in that thread mention upper-eyelid filler as a desired option that some surgeons hesitate to offer [2]. In medicine, upper-eyelid hooding is discussed mainly as an aging change, and upper blepharoplasty is the standard procedure to reduce it, so the aesthetic goal here runs opposite to the usual clinical one [4][8].

Research on eyelid appearance exists in plastic surgery: studies of what makes upper lids look attractive have examined crease height, how much of the lid shows and the position of the brow, and a pilot study found that simply tilting the head changes how the upper lid and brow look in photographs [9].

chain: Cold exposure or expression makes tissue sit over the upper lid
Eyelid appears more hooded, often temporarily
Eyes look deeper-set and more shaded
angle.text: Practitioners use ice, eyebrow-raising or, less often, fillers to add lid cover and a hooded look to the eyes. Posters describe the change as temporary and show before-and-after photos taken right after treatment.

infobox: Ice or cold water, eyebrow-raise, filler, surgery [1][2][4]
Upper-lid skin, orbital fat, brow position [4][8]

paras: The term combines "hooding" with the community suffix "-maxxing". Hooded eyes have an upper-eyelid fold that partly covers the crease; in clinical writing this is commonly linked to aging as skin elasticity and the support of the orbital septum weaken, letting redundant skin drape and fat bulge forward [4][8]. In looksmaxxing discussions some members describe a hooded look as masculine or intense and set it against "exposed" eyes with visible lid and little cover [1][3].

The aesthetic discussion overlaps with other eye-area topics in appearance culture, such as brow position, lid crease and how much pretarsal lid skin shows under the brow. A plastic surgery pilot study measured pretarsal show, upper-lid fold height and the lateral position of the brow peak and lid crease, and reported that these shift with head tilt and relate to how raters rank eye attractiveness [9].

The upper eyelid is raised by the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, and the crease forms where its aponeurosis attaches to the skin. Layers from the surface are skin, subcutaneous tissue, orbicularis oculi, the orbital septum and the tarsal plate [7][4]. The orbital septum holds back the orbital fat; with age it can weaken, allowing fat to herniate and skin to become redundant, which produces dermatochalasis and hooding [4][8].

Crease and fold patterns vary by ancestry. Wikipedia reports that single and double eyelids are polygenic traits, that the epicanthic fold is common in East and Southeast Asian populations, and that a cited study found Asian eyelids to contain more fat than White eyelids [7]. Brow position also affects hooding: a lower brow rests closer to the lid and makes the fold look heavier [4].

The guide in [1] argues that exposing the eye region to cold water increases fat storage there and that results are visible right after. A separate results thread reports short daily ice applications over two to three weeks, with the poster noting one eye changed more than the other and attributing this to the technique [3]. Other posters in the same threads said they saw little change beyond the temporary effect [1].

The theory draws on cold-exposure ideas. Brown adipose tissue is a heat-producing fat that becomes more active in the cold and, in adults, is mostly found in the supraclavicular, paravertebral and mediastinal regions rather than around the eyes [6]. Cryolipolysis, a medical technique using controlled cooling, is used to reduce localised fat in areas such as the submental region and jawline, and a rare complication called paradoxical adipose hyperplasia involves treated fat enlarging instead (reported in 0.12 to 1.0 percent of cases) [5]. Neither has been studied on eyelid fat in the manner the forum guide describes.

A poster who had written about the ice approach later recommended raising the brows and looking upward to let fat slide over the lid, saying it can last hours, and advised trying ice methods only if the eyes still look flat after that [2]. A pilot study of periorbital photographs found that head tilt alters pretarsal show, upper-lid fold height and brow peak position, and that raters judged eyes photographed with the chin slightly down as more attractive; the authors recommend controlling tilt when comparing before-and-after images [9].

Commenters mention upper-eyelid filler as an option, while noting that some oculoplastic surgeons in their countries decline to do it [2]. Upper blepharoplasty is an established procedure that removes or repositions excess skin and fat through an incision in the natural lid crease, usually as an outpatient operation lasting one to three hours with swelling and bruising that fade over several weeks [4]. It reduces hooding, so people seeking more of it do not usually turn to it; Wikipedia notes the term "blepharoplasty" was coined by Karl Ferdinand von Graefe in 1818 and that a Roman author, Celsus, described eyelid excision in the first century [4].

No studies found. No published trial has examined ice or cold exposure as a way to increase eyelid hooding. Related plastic-surgery research examines periorbital aesthetics, for example a pilot study of 12 young women in which head tilt changed upper-lid and brow measurements and attractiveness rankings [9]. Upper blepharoplasty, which does the reverse, is a standard surgical procedure [4].

Cold applied to skin can cause irritation, and eyelid fillers and surgery carry general medical risks, including bruising and swelling [4]. Excess upper-lid skin that droops over the lashes can also reduce peripheral vision, which is why clinicians treat advanced hooding surgically [4][8]. Forum posters generally describe the ice results as temporary [1][3].

timeline.event: Celsus describes an excision to relax the eyelids in De Medicina [4].
Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coins the term blepharoplasty [4].
Pilot study reports head tilt alters periorbital measurements and attractiveness ranks in photographs [9].

lore.intro: Hoodingmaxxing is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-cost eye-area trick, with ice methods shared as 'lifefuel' by members with flat upper lids.[1][3]

claims.claim: Ice on the eye area increases fat storage and causes lasting hooding
claims.believers: The guide's author says cold exposure makes the periorbital region store fat and that the change is visible immediately; another member reports results after two to three weeks.[1][3]
claims.experts: No published study has tested whether cold applied to the eyelids changes eyelid fat. Clinical literature describes eyelid hooding mainly as an age-related change.[4]

claims.claim: Raising the eyebrows lets fat settle onto the lid for hours
claims.believers: A member who tried several methods says this is easier than icing and can last for hours.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has examined this technique.

claims.claim: Cold exposure makes the eye region store fat the way it does in brown-fat theory
claims.believers: The guide's author links cold thermogenesis and brown fat to fat accumulation around the eyes [1].
claims.experts: Brown adipose tissue in adults is mostly located in the neck, upper chest and spine regions [6]; cryolipolysis uses cold to reduce, not add, local fat [5].

claims.claim: Photos showing hooding after ice reflect a real change
claims.believers: Posters share before-and-after photographs taken immediately after icing as proof [3].
claims.experts: A pilot study found head tilt alone alters pretarsal show, fold height and brow position in photographs, which is why surgeons control angle when comparing images [9].
